metadata.title: The Dollar, Exports and Factory Jobs
metadata.visual_form: Animated Cause-and-Effect Chain with Heat Stripes
metadata.data_notes: Chart starts in 2006 because the broad dollar index (DTWEXBGS) begins then.

events.label: Dollar up 16% in about a year

explanation.summary: How strong the US dollar is against other currencies, how much American goods sell abroad, and how many people work in factories that make machines, cars and equipment. The stripes below show every month since 2007: red means higher than a year before, blue means lower. A stronger dollar makes American goods more expensive abroad, so exports fall about 2 months later. Factory jobs follow exports a few months after that.
explanation.methodology: Nominal broad US dollar index from the Federal Reserve via FRED (DTWEXBGS, January 2006 = 100, monthly average). Goods exports from Census and BEA via FRED (BOPGEXP). Durable goods manufacturing jobs from BLS (CES3100000001). The chart starts in 2006, the first year of the dollar index.

key_findings.title: 2010: Factory Jobs Bottom
key_findings.description: Durable goods jobs fell from 9.02 million (June 2006) to 6.97 million in February 2010, a loss of about 2 million.
key_findings.significance: Most of these jobs never came back.

key_findings.title: 2014-2015: The Dollar Jumps
key_findings.description: The dollar rose 16% in about a year, from 97 to 113. Exports fell from $138 billion a month (October 2014) to $120 billion.
key_findings.significance: A strong dollar cuts exports quickly.

key_findings.title: January 2025: Strongest Dollar on the Chart
key_findings.description: The dollar index reached 129. Exports still rose to records, about $222 billion a month by April 2026.
key_findings.significance: Factory jobs (7.9 million as of August 2026) remain well below their 2006 level.
